slice: Live hardening — moderator termination, viewer count, recording retention, pinned ingest
register_row: INT-01 (NOT flipped — the A26 re-run decides it)
verdict: The four postures the owner ruled on after the A26 live lab are built, tested and merged-pending. A moderator (and, for the first time, the creator) can end a broadcast: the session closes, the stream key rotates, the publisher is disconnected through nginx-rtmp's control module, and the ordinary disconnect path finalises the recording into the replay. A concurrent-viewer count is derived from live playlist fetches. LIVE_RECORDING_RETENTION retires session recordings, which nothing deleted before. The ingest image is pinned by digest and a live_ingest health component now watches the RTMP plane. NOT LAB-OBSERVED: no RTMP publisher, no ingest container and no browser ran in this slice — it is code-only, and the A26 re-run is what turns these into measurements.

prs.dependency_order: core#206 changes api/openapi.yaml (the terminate route, the owner end route, viewer_count, the termination block and three new schemas), so user#200 carries the lib/api/generated.ts regen and its contract-ci cannot be green until core's spec is on main. user#200 stays a DRAFT until core#206 merges. The meta PR is independent of both.
prs.migration: core 0141_live_termination (schema 140 -> 141): terminated_at, terminated_by, termination_reason_code, termination_reason on live_streams, plus a CHECK constraint mirroring the Go allow-list. No search migration.

sc1_moderator_termination.verdict: BUILT — unit- and handler-tested; not lab-observed

routes.moderator: POST /api/v1/admin/live/{id}/terminate — requireAuth + requireRole(admin, moderator), the A16 role model every other content-moderation route takes
routes.owner: POST /api/v1/live/{id}/end — owner or channel content manager; 404 (not 403) to anyone else, matching every other owner-scoped live route. It did not exist before: the only ways off the air were stopping the encoder (which leaves the row `live` until the stop hook or the duration watchdog catches up) and DELETE, which takes the replay with it.

sequence: 1. END THE SESSION AND STORE THE REASON, in ONE statement (TerminateLiveStream). Not a flip plus an update: a crash between them would leave a stream ended with no reason — indistinguishable from an ordinary publisher disconnect — and the creator would be told nothing, which is the exact gap this closes. Live HLS 404s the moment the state is not `live` (liveStreamForHLS), the stream leaves every listing, and every playback token outstanding against it dies with it.

2. ROTATE THE STREAM KEY, before the drop. The RTMP boundary authenticates a KEY, not a session. Dropping first leaves a window in which the publisher's encoder reconnects on a credential that still works and is back on air before the rotation lands. TestTerminateRotatesBeforeDropping pins the order and fails when the two steps are swapped (verified by mutation).
3. DROP THE PUBLISHER, only now that there is nothing to reconnect to.

4. LET THE ORDINARY STOP PATH PUBLISH THE REPLAY. Terminate never calls RunReplay: the recording is still OPEN while the publisher holds the socket, so replaying it here would publish a truncated file. The drop in step 3 closes the socket, which fires the ingest's on_publish_done — the existing disconnect->replay path A26 measured working. The stop hook's re-assert of `ended` is idempotent and, by construction in SetLiveStreamState, does not clear the reason.

control_contract.auth: the X-Ingest-Secret header carrying LIVE_INGEST_SECRET — the same shared secret the hooks already present in the other direction, so an operator rotating it rotates both halves at once
control_contract.nginx: deploy/media/nginx.conf.template gains `location /control { if ($http_x_ingest_secret != …) { return 401; } rtmp_control all; }` and the same shape for /stat with rtmp_stat. `if` is the rewrite module and runs before the content phase, so a wrong or absent secret never reaches the control module. Port 8082 is NOT published to the host by the compose service, so on a default deployment only the compose network reaches it — the secret is a second layer, not the only one.
control_contract.name_is_the_id_not_the_key: The on-publish hook renames the session to the bare stream id, so after the first frame every session on the `live` application is named by its id. The raw stream key therefore never has to leave the database to end a broadcast — which is what the rename was for.
control_contract.app_is_live_not_hls: The drop targets the INGEST application. Dropping `hls` would tear down the loopback packaging push and leave the streamer connected: the audience goes dark and the publisher does not even notice. TestIngestAppIsTheIngestApplication pins the literal against the shipped template.
control_contract.ssrf_posture: LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL is an operator-configured INFRASTRUCTURE endpoint, the same class as SEARCH_SERVICE_URL and IPFS_API_URL, and is EXPECTED to be a private compose address — running it through internal/urlsafety's public-address guard would reject every correct value. Nothing request-derived reaches the URL except two query parameters: the app is a package constant and the name is a UUID's string form, both url.Values-escaped. The base URL's scheme, host and embedded credentials are validated at BOOT (internal/config), so a malformed one fails the process rather than one moderator's click. Redirects are not followed, so a misconfigured proxy's 302 cannot carry the shared secret to a third host.

sc1_moderator_termination.degrade_without_a_control_surface: No LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL: the broadcast still ends and the key is still rotated, and the response says the publisher's socket was left open rather than reporting a clean success. The api logs a WARN at boot when live is configured and the control URL is not. The config validator REFUSES a control URL with no LIVE_INGEST_SECRET — anything that can reach an unauthenticated control surface can disconnect every publisher on the instance.
sc1_moderator_termination.partial_outcomes: The response is not a 204. The three parts fail independently, and a moderator told only 'ok' while the streamer keeps uploading to the operator's disk has been misinformed at the moment it matters most. `publisher_disconnected`, `stream_key_rotated` and a `detail` sentence say which. The worst case — the state write itself failing — is the ONE failure returned as an error rather than a partial result, because it is the only one that leaves the stream ON AIR; the test asserts that neither the key rotation nor the drop ran after it.
sc1_moderator_termination.audit: content.live.terminate, with resource_id carrying the STREAM ID. A26 measured every live audit row leaving resource_id EMPTY and burying the id in free-text reason, so the audit filter could not target a stream; this row can. Reason carries the allow-listed CODE only (audit_log cannot carry prose — A16), plus the markers `publisher_not_dropped` / `key_not_rotated` when they occurred, so a partial outcome is reconstructable from the trail a week later. The moderator's free text is stored on the live_streams row, exactly where a video block stores its reason.
sc1_moderator_termination.reason_visibility: The termination block is served only to the creator, a channel content manager, or staff. NOT to the public: a takedown notice on a public page is a punishment nobody ruled on, and the moderator's words are written for the creator. TestTerminationReasonIsNotPublic asserts an anonymous visitor and a signed-in stranger get neither the block nor the free text anywhere in the body.
sc1_moderator_termination.cleared_on_the_next_go_live: SetLiveStreamState clears the four columns when a stream enters `live`, and only then. A terminated PERMANENT stream that is allowed to broadcast again must not carry last month's takedown notice on its page forever; the audit trail keeps the history, the row describes what is true now. Leaving live does NOT clear it — that is exactly when the creator needs to read it.
sc1_moderator_termination.wrong_actors: anonymous 401, ordinary user 403 on the admin route; stranger 404 on the owner route. A second terminate is 409 (`this stream is not currently live`), not 404 — the stream is real and already off, which is the outcome the caller wanted, and a 404 would send a moderator hunting for a stream sitting in front of them. Missing or unknown reason_code is 422 and does not end the broadcast.
sc1_moderator_termination.frontend: The creator sees the reason on the stream page (components/LiveWatchView.tsx) and in the Studio list (components/LiveStreamsSection.tsx), from one shared copy module (lib/live/termination.ts) so the two surfaces cannot drift. The ended-state branch keys on `termination` as well as on the state, because a terminated PERMANENT stream returns to `offline` rather than `ended`. A moderator gets an End-stream dialog on the live watch page — where a moderator watching an instance-damaging broadcast actually is — and the creator gets an End stream button in the Studio.

sc2_viewer_count.verdict: BUILT — unit-tested against an in-memory store; not lab-observed
sc2_viewer_count.signal: live HLS PLAYLIST fetches. A player refetches the playlist roughly every target duration (2 s with the shipped ingest config) for as long as it is watching and stops the moment it is not, so it is the only request in the live path that means 'still here'. Segments would measure bandwidth; GET /live/{id} would measure page views. Both the master route and the by-name route count, because a player that followed the master's own URI lands on the second.
sc2_viewer_count.identity: a keyed, day-scoped digest (internal/pseudonym) under its OWN domain label `vidra/live-viewer-digest/v1`, so a live viewer digest and a QoE viewer digest for the same person on the same day are unrelated values and the two datasets cannot be joined. A test asserts the labels differ.
sc2_viewer_count.why_not_the_qoe_session_id: The `?s=` session id was the other candidate and was rejected: it is minted by the client and sent in a body the client controls, so a count keyed on it is a count anyone can inflate by rotating a UUID. A 'concurrent viewers' number a viewer can set is worse than no number. The digest is derived server-side from the request principal and cannot be steered.
sc2_viewer_count.privacy_a35: An opted-out signed-in viewer COUNTS but leaves no account-derived value: they are digested as the anonymous visitor A13 says they asked to be treated as, through the SAME searchConsent predicate the QoE beacon uses. QoE's own rule — store the EMPTY digest — would be wrong here: the digest is a SET MEMBER, so every opted-out viewer on the instance would collapse into one member and be under-reported. Anonymous viewers are counted by the same IP-derived, keyed, day-scoped digest and never by a raw address. The value lives in Redis for the rolling window only, is never persisted, never logged, and never read back as anything but a cardinality.

window_and_refresh.why: far longer than the ~2 s playlist refresh rather than a tight multiple of it: a stalled player, a phone that locks for a moment or a congested link must not flicker out of the count and back in. The cost is that the number lags a mass exit by up to 90 s, which is the right way round — undershooting during a broadcast misleads a creator more than decaying a minute late after it.
window_and_refresh.read_refresh_why: the public 'Live now' rail renders many cards per request and must not pay a Redis round trip per card. A test asserts 50 renders inside one window cost one store read, and that the 51st after the window costs a second.

sc2_viewer_count.memory: one Redis sorted set per LIVE stream (member = digest, score = unix seconds). Every write prunes members older than the window and re-arms a TTL of window + 60 s, so a stream that stops being watched evicts itself even if it is never terminated cleanly. The read counts by range rather than ZCARD, so a stale member no write has pruned yet cannot inflate the answer. Bounded by (streams currently live) x (distinct viewers in the last window).
sc2_viewer_count.absent_not_zero: No Redis, no count: `viewer_count` is OMITTED from the projections rather than reported as 0, because 'nobody is watching' and 'this instance cannot tell' are different statements and only one belongs on a creator's page mid-broadcast. The frontend guards on `typeof === "number"`, not truthiness, so a real measured 0 still renders — a mutation to a truthy guard fails the test.
sc2_viewer_count.reset: the viewer set is dropped on the ingest stop hook and on any termination, so a PERMANENT stream going live again inside the window does not open on the previous session's tail.
sc2_viewer_count.publisher_profile_documented: 720p / 30 fps / H.264 + AAC-LC 48 kHz, passthrough, stated in vidra-core/docs/operations.md ('The supported publisher profile') and in the Studio's Go-live form. The ingest transcodes nothing — master.m3u8 for a live stream carries zero EXT-X-STREAM-INF lines and IS the media playlist — so a creator pushing 4K has not reached more people, they have made the stream unplayable for everyone without the bandwidth. Live ABR stays SCP-05.

sc3_recording_retention.verdict: BUILT — unit-tested against a real temp directory; not lab-observed
sc3_recording_retention.key: LIVE_RECORDING_RETENTION (duration, default 0). Validated at boot: negative is refused, the same mistake AUDIT_LOG_RETENTION guards, because a cutoff in the FUTURE would delete every recording on the next pass.

semantics.zero: the recording is deleted as soon as its replay VOD is published (RunReplay, success path only). The replay is then the copy — which is what the recording was an intermediate for. The retention SWEEP does nothing at 0: there is no window to enforce, and a sweep that invented one would be deleting recordings the operator never asked it to.
semantics.non_zero: nothing is deleted on publish; the sweep deletes recordings whose MTIME is older than the window. mtime and not the unix suffix in the filename, because the suffix is when the recorder OPENED the file and a long broadcast is still being written hours later.

sc3_recording_retention.failed_replay_keeps_its_recording: The delete only ever runs after Process returns successfully — every failure returns early — so a replay whose transcode failed keeps its recording, which is the only copy that broadcast will ever have. The failure log SAYS SO and names the effective retention window, so an operator reading it knows how long they have to re-transcode. TestFailedReplayKeepsTheRecording pins it.
sc3_recording_retention.worker: hourly, leader-elected, beside the QoE and audit prunes (the same jobloop cadence runTelemetryRetentionWorker uses). Its OWN loop rather than a third pass inside that one, because it touches a filesystem and not a table: a stalled NFS mount must not hold up the audit trail's retention. N replicas each unlinking the same batch would be N-1 wasted passes racing each other's ENOENT, hence the leader gate.
sc3_recording_retention.batch_why: oldest-first and bounded, the convention every other prune here follows: a volume accumulating recordings since install must not be swept in one tick that lists tens of thousands of entries and unlinks all of them. A permissions failure on one file is skipped rather than pinning the whole backlog.
sc3_recording_retention.keep_file_is_spared: the sweep never deletes `<LIVE_HLS_ROOT>/rec/.keep`. That file is load-bearing: record_path sits inside hls_path and nginx-rtmp's HLS cleanup rmdir()s empty subdirectories of it, which is why replay-to-VOD had never once run on any deployment before A26 planted it. TestRetentionSweepSparesTheKeepFile guards the regression.
sc3_recording_retention.honest_gap_at_the_default: at retention 0, two kinds of recording are never deleted by anything: a stream with replay_enabled = false (the media server records unconditionally and no replay is ever published to trigger the delete) and a replay whose transcode failed. That is the pre-existing behaviour A26 measured, unchanged — this key is the way OUT of it and a non-zero value is the way. Documented in docs/operations.md and in the env template rather than papered over with a hidden floor, because a sweep that deletes files at a threshold nobody configured is how a 'the only copy' recording disappears.
sc3_recording_retention.compose_consumer: vidra-core/docker-compose.yml's x-api-environment anchor gains LIVE_RECORDING_RETENTION and LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL, so the meta repo's 'every config key vidra-core reads has a compose consumer' gate stays green. Both are also documented in meta env/production.env.example.

sc4_pinned_ingest.before: alfg/nginx-rtmp:latest — an unpinned tag, on the one component the owner has just made launch-required, whose current build is from 2022
sc4_pinned_ingest.digest_source: the registry's own docker-content-digest header for the `latest` tag on registry-1.docker.io, read 2026-09-08. It is a single-platform manifest (application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json), consistent with A26's note that the lab ran it linux/amd64 under emulation; the tag has not moved since 2022, so this is the image that lab ran.
sc4_pinned_ingest.tag_kept_beside_the_digest: deliberate. Dependabot's docker-compose ecosystem needs a tag to know what to follow; a bare repo@sha256:… is unbumpable. The tag names what to watch, the digest is what runs.
sc4_pinned_ingest.dependabot: .github/dependabot.yml already carries the `docker-compose` ecosystem at `/`, which covers docker-compose.yml and therefore this image — the entry is annotated to say so rather than duplicated. A new `latest` now arrives as a PR to be looked at instead of as a silent change under a running instance.
sc4_pinned_ingest.meta_repo: meta pins nothing of its own here: docker-compose.prod.yml's `rtmp` block is an overlay that adds only a restart policy and a log cap on top of vidra-core's definition, and env/production.env.example carries no image reference. One pin, in one file.

sc5_ingest_component.verdict: BUILT — unit-tested with a stub prober; not lab-observed
sc5_ingest_component.component: live_ingest, on both /readyz and /admin/system (it is on the CHEAP probe componentHealth shares, so both surfaces get it)

verdicts.not_configured_no_live: LIVE_RTMP_URL unset — this install does not do live, which is a supported deployment and not a fault
verdicts.not_configured_no_control: live IS configured and LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL is not: there is an ingest and no way to ask it anything. Deliberately NOT 'ok' — the whole finding this component answers is an instance reporting health it never measured. It carries an Error sentence naming the missing key.
verdicts.down: it did not. The message says what it means for the instance; the raw transport error is NOT passed through, because it can name the ingest's address and an admin page's body travels in screenshots.

sc5_ingest_component.never_fails_readiness: a down ingest sets healthy=false so the readiness BODY reads `degraded`, and does NOT change the status CODE. handleReady 503s for PostgreSQL alone; every replica shares one ingest, so 503ing on its death would empty the whole fleet out of rotation and take the VOD platform down with the live plane.
sc5_ingest_component.probe_cost: cached for 30 s in process, so /readyz being polled several times a minute costs at most two probes a minute. A test asserts 25 readiness checks inside one window cost one probe.
sc5_ingest_component.probe_is_side_effect_free: it asks /stat and not a control command with a dummy name: a probe that runs on every readiness tick must have no side effect, and a drop request — even one that matches nothing — is a mutation aimed at whatever happens to be named that way.

sc6_gates.core: make ci (fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint, openapi-verify, sqlc-verify, test-race) — exit 0; go vet -tags=integration ./... — exit 0
sc6_gates.core_new_tests: internal/live: 20 new tests across terminate_test.go, viewers_test.go, retention_test.go and three added to replay_test.go. internal/httpapi: 9 new across admin_live_test.go and system_live_test.go. The OpenAPI contract test caught both new routes as undocumented before the spec was written, which is what it is for.
sc6_gates.core_mutation_checks: three assertions were verified to bite by breaking the code under them: swapping the rotate/drop order fails TestTerminateRotatesBeforeDropping; skipping the key rotation fails TestTerminateEndsRotatesAndDrops; a truthy viewer_count guard in the frontend fails the 'renders a real zero' test.
sc6_gates.user: npm run ci on Node 26 (typecheck, lint, lint:icons, vitest, production build, e2e) — exit 0: 258 test files / 2579 unit tests and 627 e2e tests. 14 tests in components/LiveWatchView.test.tsx (3 pre-existing, 11 added) and 5 in lib/live/termination.test.ts.
sc6_gates.meta: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p '*_test.py'; prod compose render `config -q` with the 8 dummy ${VAR:?} keys; the --profile core --profile frontend render assertions (postgres/redis/search publish no ports, api/frontend on 127.0.0.1 only); the compose-consumer assert. No script changed, so bash -n and shellcheck had nothing to lint.
sc6_gates.not_run: nothing that needs a running stack. No RTMP publisher, no ingest container, no Redis (the viewer counter is tested against an in-memory store implementing the same window semantics, and there is no -tags=integration test against a real sorted set), no browser, no /admin/system rendered by a real Postgres-backed api, and no `docker compose --profile media up`. The nginx `location /control` and `location /stat` blocks have NOT been parsed by nginx — no `nginx -t` was run against the rendered template.
sc6_gates.a_gate_that_was_claimed_before_it_passed: The first vidra-user PR pushed here claimed `npm run ci` exit 0 and it had not: the local run failed `tsc --noEmit` on the session fixture in LiveWatchView.test.tsx, and the exit code read back was the BACKGROUND WRAPPER's, not npm's. CI caught it on five lanes (frontend, ci-required, e2e-backed local + s3, channel-sync-backed all traced to the same three type errors). Recorded rather than quietly amended, because the failure mode — reading a wrapper's status as the tool's — will recur: a background job's exit code is the shell's, and the gate has to print its own. Fixed in a follow-up commit; the run reported above is a real one, after `npx playwright install chromium chromium-headless-shell` (a fresh worktree has no browser cache, which is what the second local attempt then failed on).

what_the_a26_rerun_must_prove: A real publisher, terminated by a moderator, is DISCONNECTED — ffmpeg exits, the ingest log shows the drop, and zero further bytes land in LIVE_HLS_ROOT. This is the single most important unverified claim in the slice: the control contract is read off nginx-rtmp's documented behaviour, not off the wire.

`nginx -t` accepts the rendered template, and rtmp_control / rtmp_stat are compiled into the alfg/nginx-rtmp build at the pinned digest. If they are not, /control answers 404 and every termination silently degrades to the no-control path.
The 401 gate on /control and /stat actually fires — a request with no X-Ingest-Secret, and one with a wrong value, both refused before rtmp_control runs.
The terminate -> drop -> on_publish_done -> replay chain end to end: the recording is CLOSED by the drop and the replay VOD that publishes is complete rather than truncated.
A rotated key is refused on the publisher's reconnect attempt at the real ingest (the api-level refusal is tested; the RTMP-level drop of that connection is not).
viewer_count against a real Redis and two concurrent Chromium viewers: two viewers read 2, one leaving decays to 1 within the 90 s window, and the count is 0/absent for a stream nobody is watching.
The live_ingest component reads `ok` against the running ingest and flips to `down` when the container is stopped, with /readyz still answering 200.
LIVE_RECORDING_RETENTION=0 deletes the .flv after a real replay publishes, and a non-zero window leaves it and lets the hourly sweep take it.
The pinned digest is what `docker compose --profile media up` actually pulls.
unrelated_findings: content.live.replay and content.live.force_close still leave resource_id EMPTY and put the stream id in free-text reason — the A26 finding. Only the new content.live.terminate row was fixed; the other two were left alone because changing an existing action's shape is an audit-consumer question, not a hardening one.
A hook-only flip still advertises a byte-less stream on the public 'Live now' rail (A26 finding, untouched).
There is still no live ABR ladder and nothing resyncs a drifted player to the live edge (A26 findings, SCP-05).
Live streams still have no server-generated poster, so the rail renders a decorative glyph.
